answers.children: The Dogue de Bordeaux is moderately good with children. Its gentle demeanor with loved ones allows it to tolerate toddlers and lay its massive head in a child's lap, yet its sheer size and guardian instincts mean even a friendly nudge can knock a small child over. Living with one requires constant awareness of that power inside the home.
answers.other-pets: The Dogue de Bordeaux can get along with other pets when raised together. Its protective nature and wariness of strangers extend to unfamiliar animals, while its low prey drive from guardian roots reduces chasing, but same-sex tension can appear with other large dogs. Owners must introduce new pets carefully to avoid its stubborn suspicion taking over.
answers.exercise: The Dogue de Bordeaux needs 20 to 30 minutes of walking twice daily. Short bursts of yard play suit its low-energy build descended from estate guardians rather than endurance hunters, and unmet needs lead to boredom that surfaces as destructive chewing on furniture or doors. Its massive frame overheats quickly so activity must stay moderate.
answers.shedding: Yes — the Dogue de Bordeaux sheds moderately year-round. Its short smooth coat loses hair steadily and sticks to clothing and furniture, with heavier shedding during seasonal changes that demands regular vacuuming. The single-layer texture lacks feathering yet still traps loose hair in its deep wrinkles.
answers.hypoallergenic: The Dogue de Bordeaux has a short smooth coat that sheds moderately and spreads dander around the home. Its low grooming needs mean little brushing is required, yet the breed is not among those usually suggested to allergy sufferers because no breed is genuinely hypoallergenic. (PawLabs shedding score: 6/10)
answers.training: The Dogue de Bordeaux is not easy to train. Its stubborn independence rooted in guardian and protector work means it is slow to respond to commands and requires patient, consistent leadership rather than quick biddability. The breed's loyalty shines once it accepts the handler but its massive head and deliberate pace test novice handlers daily.
answers.lifespan: The Dogue de Bordeaux lives 5-8 years. Its short lifespan ties directly to the breed's massive build and low health robustness that have challenged French breeders since the 19th century. The heavy weight and guardian history place constant physical stress on joints and heart that limit its years with family.
answers.size: The Dogue de Bordeaux reaches 99-150 lb and stands 23-27 in tall. Its massive head and powerful substance make it feel like a silent bodyguard in the house, where even casual movement can clear coffee tables. Living with one means adapting furniture and routines around a dog that occupies significant floor space yet remains gentle with its people.
answers.barking: The Dogue de Bordeaux does not bark a lot. Bred as a guardian and protector it remains quiet unless a genuine threat appears, relying instead on its deep rumbling growl and imposing presence to deter intruders. This restraint fits its French Mastiff heritage of watching estates without unnecessary noise.
answers.apartment: The Dogue de Bordeaux can live in an apartment. Its low energy and couch-potato nature let it settle indoors after short walks, while minimal barking suits shared walls, although its 150-pound frame and drooling require extra cleaning and space management. The guardian temperament stays calm provided it receives daily mental focus.
answers.first-time: The Dogue de Bordeaux is not a good first dog. Its stubbornness, protective wariness of strangers and significant health challenges demand experience that novices rarely possess, especially when managing a 150-pound dog that shadows owners yet tests boundaries daily. The loyalty rewards committed handlers but overwhelms those new to the demands.
